headline: Trump’s fresh bid for Nobel Peace Prize
snippet: Washington, Oct 08: US President Donald Trump has made a fresh bid for the Nobel Peace Prize, claiming that he had settled eight wars and “done stuff that nobody else has ever done”. Trump made the remarks at the Oval Office on Wednesday afternoon, ahead of the announcement of the coveted award on Friday by the Norwegian Peace Committee. “I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts. No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled eight wars," Trump told reporters here. The US President said it would be a great discredit to the Nobel Committee not to honour him. “They have a reputation for maybe not giving it to people like me. But, whether I get it or not, I have done far more. And I think it would be a great discredit to them. And I'm not saying that out of scorn, I'm saying that when you settle eight wars, and nobody’s never,” Trump said. The US President said his peacemaking efforts were continuing and indicated that he was on course to settle another war, an apparent reference to the US-Iran war that has now stretched into its eighth month. Trump said he deserved the award more than President Barack Obama, whom he accused of not knowing why he had received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2009. “Look, Obama got it, and he didn't do anything. He still doesn't know what he got it for. He got it when he got elected, right at the beginning, and he had no idea why he got it,” the US President said. Trump recalled that last year’s peace laureate Venezuela’s Maria Corina Machado had handed over her prize to him at the Oval Office. “Last time they gave it to a young lady who's a fabulous person, and she said she didn't deserve it, that I deserved it, and she gave it to me,” the US President said. “I was very honoured to receive it indirectly. Last time by the recipient, who said nobody in history deserves it more than President Trump,” he said. Trump repeated that in the past year he had settled eight wars, secured the return of all hostages, and prevented many wars by using the power of tariffs as a threat against certain countries, thereby stopping them from killing people.

headline: Yokohama University researchers use water as sole hydrogen source for pyridine hydrogenation
snippet: Researchers at Yokohama University have demonstrated that a carbon-supported cobalt catalyst can drive the selective hydrogenation of nitrogen-containing aromatic compounds using water as the sole hydrogen source. The system's performance hinges on a dynamic equilibrium between metallic cobalt (Co) and residual cobalt oxide (CoOx) maintained during electrolysis. Under optimized electrolysis conditions, the catalyst converted more than 99% of pyridine into piperidine, a structural unit critical to synthetic and medicinal chemistry. Mahito Atobe, Naoki Shida, and their colleagues note that catalytic efficiency is not defined by elemental composition alone, but by how the oxidation state of cobalt shifts directly within the reaction environment. In situ X-ray spectroscopy and theoretical calculations revealed that the optimal ratio of Co(0) to CoOx facilitates pyridine adsorption and subsequent hydrogenation. An excess of either form diminishes catalytic activity. This mechanism suppresses unwanted reaction pathways often observed with more expensive rhodium-based catalysts.

headline: Marina Bay Sands Expands Wildlife Conservation Efforts
snippet: In late July, Marina Bay Sands announced a three-year commitment of more than $1.1 million to the Mandai Wildlife Centre, Singapore’s newest facility dedicated to rehabilitating rescued native wildlife. The contribution represents one of the resort’s most significant investments in biodiversity conservation to date. It underscores Marina Bay Sands’ ongoing focus on safeguarding wildlife, enhancing ecosystem resilience and advancing its wider sustainability objectives. Managed by Mandai Nature, the nonprofit conservation arm of Mandai Wildlife Group, the facility has been specifically designed to provide better care and rehabilitation outcomes for Singapore’s rescued native animals. It also serves as a platform for research and the development of expertise in wildlife medicine, veterinary care and conservation. Over the three-year partnership, Marina Bay Sands and Mandai Nature will also take conservation education beyond the rehabilitation facility. Together, they plan to create customized experiences and educational opportunities for international visitors and community partners, helping participants better understand wildlife conservation and the need to protect biodiversity within urban environments. “We are delighted to support partners such as Mandai Nature in protecting Singapore’s native biodiversity,” said Meridith Beaujean, assistant vice president of sustainability and ESG at Marina Bay Sands. She noted that as a major hospitality destination, the resort relies on healthy ecosystems and rich biodiversity to create environments that people value and enjoy. She added that supporting the center reflects the company’s view that the long-term success of destinations and wildlife conservation are interconnected, while also recognizing the hospitality industry’s responsibility to make a meaningful contribution to both. The contribution to the Mandai Wildlife Centre is the latest in a series of collaborations developed by Sands and its regional operations to promote sustainability, conservation and environmental education. These partnerships are supported by the Sands ECO360 global sustainability team, which works on issues including emissions reduction, responsible water management, waste minimization, sustainable materials and resource use, and biodiversity conservation. Expanding Sustainability Through Cross-Disciplinary Initiatives Earlier in the summer, Marina Bay Sands announced a two-year collaboration with the SG Eco Fund aimed at increasing public awareness and encouraging community participation in environmental sustainability and climate resilience initiatives in Singapore. The partnership began on June 11 with a special screening of trailers from the Sustainable Futures Film Festival at ArtScience Museum. The festival, which runs through Aug. 31, features films examining climate change and biodiversity conservation. The film program supports Singapore’s Year of Climate Adaptation, an initiative focused on increasing awareness of climate-related impacts while bringing together perspectives from art, science and sustainability. The launch event also provided complimentary exhibition booths for SG Eco Fund recipients Witteveen+Bos, Pasarfish and PUB, Singapore’s National Water Agency. The organizations presented projects designed to strengthen Singapore’s climate resilience, including initiatives involving food security as well as flood and coastal protection. Established in 2020 and administered by Singapore’s Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment, the $39 million SG Eco Fund provides financial support for community-led projects that promote environmental sustainability. The Marina Bay Sands-SG Eco Fund partnership will also introduce interactive exhibitions at ArtScience Museum focused on biodiversity and sustainability. The resort plans to work with SG Eco Fund recipients to incorporate exhibition booths, artistic installations, educational tours and practical sustainability workshops designed for students and members of the public. Advancing Conservation Through Responsible Hospitality Marina Bay Sands has maintained a partnership with World Wide Fund for Nature Singapore since 2015. The relationship initially concentrated on responsible seafood procurement but has since expanded into a broader effort to encourage more sustainable practices across the resort’s supply chain. The collaboration includes traceability assessments as well as improvement initiatives involving aquaculture and fisheries across the region. Marina Bay Sands is currently working with the nonprofit organization to examine how the hospitality sector is connected to deforestation risks within supply chains. As part of the effort, the resort conducted a detailed assessment of deforestation and land-conversion risks across its supply chain, concentrating on commodities considered particularly exposed to these risks, including palm oil, cocoa, coffee, beef, soy, paper and timber. The assessment examined procurement information and involved discussions with suppliers about their sourcing methods, certifications and traceability systems. This work established a baseline of potential risks and opportunities. Drawing on international frameworks and established best practices, the initiative aims to improve supply-chain transparency, increase understanding of deforestation-related risks and encourage suppliers to identify ways to reduce deforestation and move toward sourcing that avoids harmful land conversion. Marina Bay Sands also began collaborating last year with conservation organization Hutan on a program designed to restore wildlife corridors within palm oil plantation landscapes in Sabah, Malaysian Borneo. Hutan’s reforestation efforts are intended to restore habitats used by endangered wildlife. As part of the initiative, Marina Bay Sands funded the work of four Indigenous Orang Sungei women for one year, covering their salaries, benefits and operational expenses as members of Hutan’s reforestation team. The model supports continued ecological restoration while creating sustainable employment opportunities for women and reflects the integrated resort’s broader regenerative approach to hospitality. The Drop By Drop Project One of Sands’ longest-running sustainability collaborations is its partnership with The WASH Foundation through The Drop By Drop Project. The initiative provides grants for innovative water-management and conservation programs in Macao and Singapore, with a focus on improving water resilience, restoring ecosystems, developing new water-related solutions and involving local communities. In Macao, the University of Saint Joseph (USJ) is currently receiving support through the program. Its funding is being used for the Sponge City Macao project, which investigates how mangrove restoration can be combined with sponge-city concepts to establish a more sustainable approach to urban water management. The project combines scientific research with community participation and seeks to improve flood preparedness, increase the retention of stormwater and promote long-term ecological stability within Macao’s urban environment. The Drop By Drop Project is also supporting two initiatives in the broader Singapore region. Reef Check Malaysia has received funding for its Mabul Clean Water Initiative. The project provides sustainable and secure water supplies through rainwater-harvesting systems for 100 low-income households on Mabul Island in Sabah. One of its key objectives is to reduce the community’s reliance on expensive imported water. The project is also funding The International SeaKeepers Society’s Orang Seletar Sungai Temon Project. The initiative supports the Indigenous Orang Seletar community as it works to restore a storm-damaged community hall and conduct water-quality monitoring in response to declining mussel yields. Together, these activities aim to preserve the community’s cultural heritage, strengthen local environmental stewardship and improve long-term economic resilience. Supporting Sustainable Seafood Practices Sands China has been a member of the Hong Kong Sustainable Seafood Coalition (HKSSC), an organization working to expand the sustainable seafood market across Hong Kong, Macao and the wider region through responsible sourcing. Most recently, Sands China contributed to HKSSC’s World Oceans Day outreach on June 8 by introducing specially selected sustainable seafood dishes at four Sands China restaurants. Marina Bay Sands also participated in the coalition’s World Oceans Day awareness initiative at RISE, its signature buffet restaurant. “We’ve aligned with these leading environmental organizations because we are committed to advancing sustainability in all aspects of our business and in our regions,” said Katarina Tesarova, senior vice president and chief sustainability officer. She explained that the partnerships enable Sands to strengthen its environmental stewardship while helping partner organizations broaden their reach and further their conservation missions. According to Tesarova, the relationships have created mutual benefits, with the shared objective of developing more effective approaches to protecting ecosystems and conserving natural resources across the regions where Sands operates. headline: The Games That Tell Palestine’s Story: A Fight to Keep Heritage Alive
snippet: JENIN, West Bank / PNN — In an effort to prevent traditional Palestinian games from being forgotten, Samahear Al-Roumi, director of the “Bayt Al-Dammah” centre for reviving Palestinian folk games in the town of Zababdeh in Jenin governorate, is documenting the games, introducing them to younger generations and reconnecting them with the history, culture, customs and traditions of Palestinian towns and villages. Al-Roumi said Bayt Al-Dammah was established as a space dedicated to preserving Palestinian folk games from disappearing, explaining that the project brings together three main categories of traditional games. The first category includes games that rely on thinking and strategy, such as Al-Dammah, Al-Sijah and Mancala. The second consists of movement-based games, including Seven Stones, Abu Asfourah, also known as Al-Habi, Al-Hila and Hopscotch. Al-Roumi noted that some games are known by different names in different parts of Palestine. The third category includes games that document Palestinian cities and villages that were depopulated, with each game linked to a particular city and the villages associated with it. Among them are games representing Acre and its villages, Haifa and its villages, Safed and others. A game with a story and a lesson Al-Roumi said every game at Bayt Al-Dammah carries information and a story connected to a particular place and to Palestinian heritage, helping visitors learn about their own villages or cities, as well as their culture and traditions. She cited the example of the Olive Press game, which is linked to an olive press in Sebastia, known for its olive trees and traditional olive presses. Through the game, visitors first learn about the history of the place before playing it themselves. The aim, she said, goes beyond simply playing traditional games. Instead, the project seeks to turn each game into a gateway to Palestinian history, geography and heritage. Al-Roumi said the design and colours of Bayt Al-Dammah were inspired by the oranges of Haifa and Jaffa, adding that the centre seeks to create a space where Palestinian visitors can experience a connection with the simpler way of life that existed decades ago. She described it as a return to a time when Palestinians relied heavily on local resources, surrounded by mulberry, fig and pomegranate trees and za'atar, as well as wells and small farms — reflecting a rural way of life built largely on self-reliance. Shortlisted among hundreds of projects Al-Roumi said Bayt Al-Dammah was selected from among 293 projects and reached the qualifying stage of an event in Jordan attended by Princess Dana Firas. The project was also documented in a dedicated festival catalogue. Every Sunday afternoon, Bayt Al-Dammah welcomes children and their mothers, allowing them to play traditional games together. The centre also accepts bookings from institutions, charities, universities and other organisations wishing to organise visits or activities. The project’s activities are not confined to the centre. Al-Roumi said the games can also be transported and used at festivals, conferences and other events. Older generations discover games they never knew were Palestinian The surprise is not limited to children, Al-Roumi said. Some visitors over the age of 50 have discovered for the first time that games they encounter at Bayt Al-Dammah are, in fact, longstanding Palestinian folk games. The initiative introduces visitors to the history of the games, some of which date back to earlier historical periods. Others were introduced to the Levant during the Ottoman era. Each game has its own history and context, which the centre's management explains to visitors. Bayt Al-Dammah also sells a number of Palestinian traditional games in an effort to keep them present in homes and among children and younger generations, rather than limiting their use to heritage events. From traditional preservation to digital archiving Al-Roumi said preserving Palestinian folk games requires moving towards a new stage of documentation. She highlighted the need to produce a specialised catalogue of Palestinian traditional games containing the games themselves, their rules, their history and information about the Palestinian regions with which they are associated. She also stressed the importance of digitally archiving the games, calling on universities and specialist students — including students and graduates in artificial intelligence — to work with the project to document and preserve the games through digital tools capable of bringing Palestinian heritage to a wider audience around the world. The project's primary goal, she said, is to prevent Palestinian folk games from disappearing because they form part of Palestinian memory, culture and identity, and to pass them from one generation to another through practice, documentation and an understanding of their history. **This video was produced with financial support from CFI, Expertise France and the European Union.
